title: Job 11:13–20
context: Zophar, continuing his first speech, urges Job to set his heart right, stretch out his hands to God, and put away iniquity, promising security, hope, and restored honor, and closes with a warning about the end of the wicked. His counsel contains truths about repentance and hope, but it assumes that Job’s suffering proves hidden sin, an assumption the book rejects (1:8; 42:7). Both traditions read the passage as shared ground, reporting Zophar’s counsel as a friend’s words rather than the book’s verdict.

verses.text: “If you set your heart aright, stretch out your hands toward him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar tells Job that if he sets his heart right, he should stretch out his hands to God. He calls for repentance.

Arminian readers note that turning to God is good counsel in itself, though Zophar assumes Job’s guilt.
verses.reformedNotes:
The advice is sound in general but misdirected here, since the prologue shows Job is not suffering for sin.

Reformed readers see a true call to repentance wrongly applied. Both traditions read this as shared ground about counsel that must fit the person.

verses.text: If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away. Don’t let unrighteousness dwell in your tents.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar urges Job to put away any iniquity and not let wickedness dwell in his tents. He presses his charge.

Arminian readers see good counsel in principle, still shaped by Zophar’s assumption that Job’s suffering proves hidden sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
The words are true as general moral teaching but presuppose a guilt the book does not attribute to Job.

Reformed readers see a friend’s counsel that misjudges. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report it as Zophar’s words, not the book’s verdict on Job.

verses.text: Surely then you will lift up your face without spot. Yes, you will be steadfast, and will not fear,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar promises that Job will then lift his face without blemish, steadfast and unafraid. Restoration is offered.

Arminian readers see hope held out, though tied to a repentance Job has no reason to offer.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar’s promises sound attractive but rest on a simple formula of sin and suffering that the book challenges.

Reformed readers see well-meant hope built on a flawed premise. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the limits of the friends’ theology.

verses.text: for you will forget your misery. You will remember it like waters that have passed away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says Job will forget his misery and remember it like waters that have passed away. The image is gentle.

Arminian readers note the beauty of the promise while recognizing its conditional basis in Zophar’s argument.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of passing waters is vivid and hopeful.

Reformed readers see in it a true hope that God can bring, though Zophar ties it to Job’s confession of guilt. Both traditions read this as shared ground; the book’s ending does restore Job, but on different terms.

verses.text: Life will be clearer than the noonday. Though there is darkness, it will be as the morning.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar promises that life will shine brighter than noon and darkness will become morning. Light replaces gloom.

Arminian readers see hope offered in answer to the darkness of Job’s lament in 10:21–22, though on Zophar’s terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Zophar’s picture contrasts directly with Job’s closing words about darkness.

Reformed readers see a hope that is true in God but offered on mistaken conditions. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hear Zophar’s promise within the book’s larger story.

verses.text: You will be secure, because there is hope. Yes, you will search, and will take your rest in safety.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says Job will be secure because there is hope, and will rest in safety. Security is promised.

Arminian readers see hope as a gift from God, though Zophar makes it depend on Job admitting guilt he has not committed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hope is a central theme in Job, and the book itself will show God restoring him.

Reformed readers see true security grounded in God, not in a formula. Both traditions read this as shared ground about hope rightly placed in God.

verses.text: Also you will lie down, and no one will make you afraid. Yes, many will court your favor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says Job will lie down without fear, and many will seek his favor. Honor will return.

Arminian readers see Zophar describing restored standing among people, a picture that the book’s ending partly echoes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise of renewed honor anticipates themes in chapter 42, though Zophar’s conditions differ from the book’s actual resolution.

Reformed readers see God as the giver of honor. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not overpress the parallel.

verses.text: But the eyes of the wicked will fail. They will have no way to flee. Their hope will be the giving up of the spirit.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar ends by warning that the eyes of the wicked will fail, with no escape and no hope but death. The speech closes with threat.

Arminian readers see an implied warning aimed at Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
The warning is true of persistent wickedness, but Zophar’s application to Job is part of what 42:7 rebukes.

Reformed readers see a sound principle misapplied. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report it as Zophar’s words.
